questions.explanation: Convexity is the segment test: for every pair of points in \(C\) and every weight \(t \in [0, 1]\), the combination \((1-t)x + ty\) is in \(C\). A union of two balls can fail that test. The origin is not required, and a half-space is convex and unbounded.

questions.prompt: What is the first coordinate of the midpoint of \((2, 10)\) and \((8, 4)\)?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is \(\tfrac12(2+8, 10+4) = (5, 7)\). The first coordinate is 5. The second coordinate is 7. Either endpoint alone would give 2 or 8. If a convex set contains both endpoints, it contains this midpoint.

questions.prompt: Which operation preserves convexity for every family of convex sets?
questions.explanation: A point in the intersection lies in every set of the family, so the segment between two such points lies in every set, hence in the intersection. A union of two disjoint disks fails, because a bridge between them leaves both disks. The boundary of a disk is a circle, which is not convex. The complement of a disk is not convex either.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to prove that a closed half-space \(\{x : a^T x \le b\}\) is convex.
questions.explanation: The combination has to be built before its image under \(a^T\) can be expanded. The expansion is a weighted average of two numbers that are each at most \(b\), so the average is at most \(b\). The algebra \((1-t)b + tb = b\) is the last simplification. Bounding before the combination exists has nothing to bound. Replacing the upper bound \(b\) by a sum \(a^T x + a^T y\) would be a looser and different claim.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>line with one side shaded</title><line x1="36" y1="168" x2="250" y2="168"/><polygon points="250,168 243.6,170.7 243.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="184" x2="48" y2="22"/><polygon points="48,22 50.7,28.4 45.3,28.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="244" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="18" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><polygon points="70,150 210,40 250,40 250,170 70,170" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.15"/><line x1="60" y1="158" x2="220" y2="30" stroke-width="2.2"/></svg>

steps: Take two points \(x\) and \(y\) in the half-space, and a weight \(t \in [0, 1]\).
Split \(a^T z\) into \((1-t)\, a^T x + t\, a^T y\).
Replace each of \(a^T x\) and \(a^T y\) by its upper bound \(b\).
Simplify \((1-t)b + tb\) to \(b\), which is the half-space inequality for \(z\).

questions.prompt: On the segment from \((0, 0)\) to \((8, 12)\), the point at \(t = 1/4\) has what second coordinate?
questions.explanation: The point is \((1-t)(0, 0) + t(8, 12)\). At \(t = 1/4\) the second coordinate is \(12/4 = 3\). The first coordinate is 2. The endpoint value 12 would be \(t = 1\). A convex set that contains both endpoints contains this point.

questions.prompt: Both \((2, 1)\) and \((4, 3)\) lie in \(\{x : x_1 + 2 x_2 \le 10\}\). What is the left-hand side at their midpoint?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is \((3, 2)\). The left-hand side is \(3 + 2 \cdot 2 = 7\), which is at most 10, so the midpoint stays in the half-space. At the first point the left-hand side is 4, and at the second it is 10. The average of 4 and 10 is also 7, which is the same computation because the constraint is linear.

questions.prompt: Which of these sets are convex?
questions.explanation: A closed half-space passes the segment test because a linear inequality is preserved by averages. An open ball of any norm does too: the triangle inequality and absolute homogeneity keep a combination inside the ball. A hyperplane is an affine set, and affine sets are convex. The union of two disjoint disks fails as soon as the segment between them crosses the gap. A circle fails because the chord between two of its points leaves the circle.

an open ball of any norm
the union of two disjoint closed disks

questions.prompt: A convex set that contains \((0, 0)\), \((8, 0)\), and \((0, 8)\) contains the combination with weights \(1/2\), \(1/4\), and \(1/4\) in that order. What is the first coordinate of that combination?
questions.explanation: The combination is \(\tfrac12(0, 0) + \tfrac14(8, 0) + \tfrac14(0, 8) = (2, 2)\). The first coordinate is 2. The second coordinate is also 2, from the third point. The weight \(1/2\) on the origin contributes nothing. Convexity for pairs extends to any finite convex combination, which is why this point has to belong to the set.

questions.prompt: One of these steps is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails.
questions.explanation: Each disk is convex, and a segment that starts and ends inside one disk does stay there. The last step only applies the general claim above it. That claim is false: convexity of the union also requires segments that start in one disk and end in the other. Those segments cross the gap and leave the union. The disks themselves are convex, so the failure is not in the first geometric step, and the union is not empty.

questions.figure_alt: Two filled disks with a gap between them.
steps: Let A and B be closed disks with a gap between them.
Each of A and B is convex.
A union of convex sets is convex, because a segment that starts and ends in one of them stays in that one.
Applying that claim to A and B says that their union is convex.
reasons: A segment from a point of A to a point of B can cross the gap and leave the union.
Disks are not convex, so the claim that each disk is convex is the false step.
The union of two nonempty sets is empty, so the last step has no set to discuss.

questions.prompt: A polyhedron, defined by finitely many linear inequalities, is
questions.explanation: Each linear inequality describes a half-space, and an intersection of half-spaces is convex. Vertices do not cancel that. The inequalities that define a polyhedron are closed, not strict. A polyhedron can be unbounded, so it is not a ball in general. Extreme points of that convex set are the next object.

convex, because it is an intersection of half-spaces

questions.prompt: Both \((0, 0)\) and \((4, 2)\) lie in \(\{x : x_1 + 2 x_2 \le 8, \; x \ge 0\}\). What is \(x_1 + 2 x_2\) at their midpoint?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is \((2, 1)\), and \(2 + 2 \cdot 1 = 4\), which is at most 8. The endpoint \((4, 2)\) gives 8, and the origin gives 0. The average of those two values is 4, matching the linear constraint. The segment test is what later lets a local minimizer over a convex set be global.

questions.prompt: The domain of a convex function has to be
questions.explanation: The chord definition compares values at the endpoints of a segment with the value at the combination, so the combination has to lie in the domain. The domain is therefore a convex set. An open nonconvex set cannot be a domain. Sublevel sets of a convex function are convex, but the domain is the set on which the function is defined, not a union chosen after the fact. Local minimizers are a subset of the domain.
